cards.title: Shortest runs in 3-D VASS
cards.formal: Is there no single-exponential bound on shortest runs in binary-encoded three-dimensional vector addition systems with states? Precisely, is it true that for every integer k≥1, every real C>0 and every N₀≥1, there is a reachable instance I of encoding length N≥N₀ whose shortest source-to-target run has more than 2^(C N^k) transitions?
cards.why: Isolates how much witness complexity three unbounded counters can force. Resolving the single-exponential threshold would clarify the gap between low-dimensional reachability and the much more expensive behavior possible when the number of counters grows.
cards.status_note: Original question and the 2025 explicit binary formulation checked, with subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026. The July 2026 preprint improves the upper bound but does not resolve whether single-exponential shortest runs always suffice. No resolution of that threshold was located; proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: Czerwiński asks for a three-counter shortest-run lower bound beyond the exponential scale; the upper-bound discussion is historical.
The ICALP paper obtains a triple-exponential shortest-run upper bound and 2-EXPSPACE membership. Section 7 retains the question whether single-exponential runs suffice for binary 3-VASS.

Chen and coauthors state a doubly-exponential shortest-run upper bound and EXPSPACE membership in a new preprint. This review checked the model and theorem statements, not the full proof; the result does not supply the requested super-single-exponential lower bound.

sentences: A three-dimensional VASS is a finite-state system with three nonnegative integer counters.
The source asks whether some reachable instances require shortest runs longer than every single-exponential bound in their binary input length.
Encoding a large initial counter in binary already permits exponentially many necessary steps, so a stronger growth rate is required.
A July 2026 preprint states a doubly-exponential upper bound, improving the triple-exponential bound from 2025.
The remaining threshold question measures how much reachability-witness complexity three counters can force.

cards.definitions: A three-dimensional vector addition system with states (3-VASS) is a finite set Q of control states and a finite transition set T⊆Q×ℤ³×Q. A configuration is (q,u) with q∈Q and u∈ℕ³, where ℕ includes zero. A transition (q,a,q′) sends (q,u) to (q′,u+a) only when every coordinate of u+a is nonnegative. There are no zero tests or counter bounds. A reachability instance I consists of Q,T and two configurations s,t. It is reachable if some finite sequence of enabled transitions sends s to t. Its shortest-run length ℓ(I) is the minimum number of transitions in such a sequence; the empty run is allowed, and ℓ(I)=0 when s=t. Unreachable instances are excluded from the quantified claim. N is the bit length of an explicit description: states are numbered, the transition list and the source and target are given explicitly, and all integer coordinates are written in signed binary (nonnegative binary for configurations), with delimiters and state indices included. Usual explicit binary-list encodings differ by polynomial factors, which do not affect existence of a 2^(N^O(1)) bound. The dimension is always exactly three, while the number of states, transitions and counter magnitudes may grow. No finite-reachability-set promise or effective construction of the hard instances is required. The single-exponential convention and binary encoding follow the explicit later formulation in Section 7 of the 2025 source.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed unboundedness beyond every 2^(C N^k), or refute it by proving that there are fixed C>0 and integer k≥1 for which every reachable binary 3-VASS instance I has ℓ(I)≤2^(C |I|^k), after adjusting C to include the finitely many small sizes. A long run alone is insufficient: the lower bound concerns the shortest run between the chosen configurations. Neither a lower bound with a growing number of counters nor the mere existence of many reachable configurations establishes this target.

context_blocks.title: Three counters, infinitely many configurations
context_blocks.text: The control graph is finite, but each counter may become arbitrarily large. A transition can consume tokens from one counter and produce tokens in another, provided it never makes a counter negative. Reachability asks whether a target configuration can be obtained from a given start through legal transitions.

context_blocks.title: Why the binary encoding matters
context_blocks.text: Consider one state and the single transition (−1,+1,0), from counters (2^r,0,0) to (0,2^r,0). Every successful run has exactly 2^r steps, although the instance uses only O(r) bits. This gives exponential length in the input description. The question asks whether shortest runs can exceed every bound 2^(N^k), with fixed k, rather than merely whether exponential runs occur.

context_blocks.title: Shortest paths control witness size
context_blocks.text: A reachable target may have many very long runs leading to it. Only the minimum length is relevant here. A single-exponential shortest-run upper bound would allow the binary reachability problem to be decided in polynomial space, as the 2025 source explains. A lower bound on the number or largest size of reachable configurations is a different assertion.

context_blocks.title: The known upper bound has changed
context_blocks.text: The 2019 question mentioned a tower-type upper bound. The ICALP 2025 work gives a triple-exponential bound on shortest runs, and the July 2026 preprint states an improvement to a doubly-exponential bound. These upper bounds do not establish that any shortest run actually needs more than single-exponential length.

cards.title: Oracle separation of BQP from IP
cards.formal: Does there exist a classical Boolean oracle A and a language L⊆{0,1}* such that L∈BQP^A but L∉IP^A?
cards.why: Determines whether classical single-prover verification of efficient quantum computations survives arbitrary oracle access. The distinction is sharper than a quantum speedup over direct classical computation: even an unrestricted interactive helper must fail in the separating world.
cards.status_note: Source Problems 7–8 and the April 2026 paper checked; subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026 located no resolution of the stated oracle question. The MIP containment changes the prover model and is recorded as preprint progress. This is a formulation and source review, not an exhaustive literature or proof audit.

progress.text: Aaronson states the oracle separation as Problem 7 and defines the distinction between IP and its efficient-quantum-honest-prover variant.

The preprint A Relativizing MIP for BQP states containment in classical MIP for every classical oracle and explicitly leaves the single-prover oracle separation open. The introduction also identifies efficient-honest-prover verification as an open issue. This review checked the statements and model, not the full proofs.

cards.definitions: An oracle is an arbitrary fixed Boolean function A:{0,1}*→{0,1}; it need not be computable. All languages are subsets of {0,1}*, and n is the input length. A classical oracle call supplies one string z and returns A(z). Quantum access uses the unitary |z,b⟩↦|z,b⊕A(z)⟩, extended linearly to superpositions of strings of a given length. Query registers and the work required to prepare them count toward the computation bound. No quantum-valued oracle, advice string or promise on inputs is supplied. BQP^A consists of languages decided by one uniform quantum algorithm with polynomial total running time, oracle calls and qubits. On every yes input it accepts with probability at least 2/3, and on every no input with probability at most 1/3. One standard machine convention uses Hadamard H=(1/√2)[[1,1],[1,−1]], T=diag(1,e^(iπ/4)) and CNOT |a,b⟩↦|a,a⊕b⟩ gates, zero-initialized auxiliary qubits, computational-basis measurements and polynomial-time classical control. Circuit descriptions are generated uniformly in polynomial time; there is no nonuniform advice. Probabilities are over measurements and any internal random bits. An IP^A protocol has one classical probabilistic polynomial-time verifier and one prover, exchanging only classical bit strings. The verifier has private fair random bits and classical access to A. Its total computation, random bits, communication and number of rounds are bounded by a polynomial in n, with no predetermined universal degree. Completeness requires one honest prover strategy that makes the verifier accept with probability at least 2/3 on every yes input. Soundness requires acceptance probability at most 1/3 on every no input against every prover strategy, including computationally unbounded strategies. The prover knows the common input and oracle but not the verifier’s unrevealed private coins; its messages can depend on its conversation history. There is no trusted setup or shared entanglement. Prover efficiency is unrestricted in IP^A. Probabilities include verifier randomness and any randomness or measurements of the prover.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of one oracle A and language L with the stated separation, ruling out every polynomial-time classical interactive proof for L relative to A. Alternatively, prove BQP^A⊆IP^A for every classical Boolean oracle A. A lower bound for a fixed round limit does not by itself exclude all polynomial-round protocols.

context_blocks.title: Can a classical verifier trust a quantum computation?
context_blocks.text: A quantum computer might efficiently decide a language while a classical computer cannot directly reproduce its calculation. An interactive proof lets the verifier ask questions and test the answers. This card asks whether even an all-powerful helper can always make the quantum answer classically checkable when both sides must use a supplied oracle through its query interface.

context_blocks.title: The same function, different query access
context_blocks.text: The quantum computation may query a superposition, whereas the verifier queries one ordinary string at a time. The oracle function itself is identical for both. Some oracle languages are easy for both: for L={x:A(x)=1}, the verifier simply queries x. The question requires a language whose quantum computation cannot be certified by the stated interaction.

context_blocks.title: Two distinct single-prover questions
context_blocks.text: For every oracle, IP_BQP^A⊆BQP^A and IP_BQP^A⊆IP^A by definition. An oracle separation of BQP from unrestricted-prover IP therefore also separates BQP from IP_BQP. The efficient-honest-prover separation is a weaker demand: an unrestricted prover might still verify that language. The two cards record this implication without identifying the targets.

context_blocks.title: Unbounded cheating is part of the guarantee
context_blocks.text: The prover can lie in any computationally possible way, even with unlimited computation. Restricting only a dishonest prover to efficient strategies would instead describe a computationally sound argument. Cryptographic verification protocols with that guarantee do not establish the information-theoretic IP containment requested here.

context_blocks.title: What the 2026 multiple-prover result changes
context_blocks.text: Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi state BQP^A⊆MIP^A for every classical oracle. MIP permits several separated provers who cannot communicate during the protocol; the stated result uses classical provers without shared entanglement. The source still identifies the single-prover oracle question as open and does not supply a polynomial-time quantum honest prover for its MIP result.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
